Spatial Analysis of Pneumonia Mortality in Korea

Keywords: pneumonia mortality, spatiotemporal analysis, Moran’s I, Bayesian hierarchical model, INLA, BYM, South Korea

SummaryDataRegressionSpatial clustering Bayesian models2015–2019Conclusion

Summary

Pneumonia is now the third leading cause of death in Korea. This analysis asks two questions: is municipal pneumonia mortality spatially clustered, and which community-level factors explain the differences between municipalities?

Global Moran’s I
0.447
p = 0.001. Mortality is positively spatially autocorrelated.
Financial independence
RR 0.85
95% CrI 0.77–0.93 per 1 SD. Protective (BYM model).
Hypertension prevalence
RR 1.12
95% CrI 1.03–1.21 per 1 SD. Risk factor (BYM model).
Best-fitting model
BYM
DIC 2228 vs 2458 (Besag) and 2488 (non-spatial).
  • Clustering. Mortality is spatially structured. High-high clusters sit in the north-east and central parts of the country (LISA map, below).
  • Determinants. Older mean age and lower population density are associated with higher mortality. Lower financial independence and higher hypertension prevalence remain associated with higher mortality after spatial smoothing.
  • Trend. In the 2015–2019 model, expected deaths rise about 14% per year (RR 1.14 per year, 95% CrI 1.13–1.15).

Data and methods

The outcome is the 2019 age-standardised pneumonia mortality rate (per 100,000) for each of Korea’s 250 municipalities, together with the number of deaths. Explanatory variables cover four domains: physical environment (PM10, household and workplace passive smoking), socioeconomic (financial independence, education below high school, proportion single), behavioural (smoking, high-risk drinking, regular exercise, obesity, hypertension, diabetes) and healthcare (doctors per 1,000, unmet medical needs). Population density, sex ratio and mean age were used as covariates. 2019 data were used to avoid distortion from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Negative binomial regression


The outcome is overdispersed relative to a Poisson distribution (observed/theoretical variance = 1.83, p < 0.001), so negative binomial models were used, with log(population) as an offset and standardised predictors (rate ratios are per 1 SD).


1. Univariable screening


Each variable was tested alone; those with p < 0.25 (shaded) were carried forward. Passive smoking at work, high-risk drinking and unmet medical needs were screened out.

2. Multivariable model and final model


The 11 screened variables plus the three covariates entered a multivariable model. Collinearity was acceptable (all VIF < 10; highest were mean age 6.2 and education 4.4). Backward elimination on AIC then gave the final model.

library(sp); library(spdep); library(sf); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr)
library(MASS); library(car); library(DHARMa); library(tmap); library(INLA)

su <- read.csv("Pnuemonia_newver.csv", header = TRUE, as.is = TRUE)
colnames(su) <- c("SIG_CD","Pop_2019","sex_ratio_19","m_age_2017","Highrisk_drk_2019",
  "smk_cur_p_2019","Passive_smk_househ_2019","Passive_smk_workpl_2019","Reg_exercise_2019",
  "Per_below_highsch_2019","Fin_ind_2019","Perc_Single_2019","doc_per1000_17",
  "Percent_hypertension_2019","Percent_diabetes_2019","Obesity_prev_2019",
  "Unmet_medical_facilities_2019","PM10_2019","Pneumonia19","Pneumonia_deaths",
  "Population_density_19","Old_age_popn")

# descriptive statistics
vars <- c("Highrisk_drk_2019","smk_cur_p_2019","Passive_smk_househ_2019","Passive_smk_workpl_2019",
  "Reg_exercise_2019","Per_below_highsch_2019","Fin_ind_2019","Perc_Single_2019","doc_per1000_17",
  "Percent_hypertension_2019","Percent_diabetes_2019","Obesity_prev_2019",
  "Unmet_medical_facilities_2019","PM10_2019","Pneumonia19","Pneumonia_deaths")

ggplot(su, aes(x = Pneumonia19)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), color = "black", fill = "#0099F8") +

R code · the regression models
# overdispersion of the outcome
library(qcc)
qcc.overdispersion.test(su$Pneumonia19[!is.na(su$Pneumonia19)], type = "poisson")

# standardise explanatory variables (mean 0, SD 1)
su[, c(3:18, 21)] <- sapply(su[, c(3:18, 21)], scale)

# univariable negative binomial models, offset = log(population)
covar <- su[, 5:18]
res <- t(sapply(covar, function(x) {
  m <- summary(glm.nb(Pneumonia_deaths ~ x + offset(log(Pop_2019)), data = su, link = log))
  c(coefficient = m$coefficients[2, 1], pval = m$coefficients[2, 4])
}))
res[res[, "pval"] < 0.25, ]          # variables carried into the multivariable model

# multivariable model, collinearity check, backward elimination on AIC
b1 <- glm.nb(Pneumonia_deaths ~ Passive_smk_househ_2019 + PM10_2019 + Fin_ind_2019 +
  Per_below_highsch_2019 + Perc_Single_2019 + smk_cur_p_2019 + Reg_exercise_2019 +
  Percent_hypertension_2019 + Percent_diabetes_2019 + Obesity_prev_2019 + doc_per1000_17 +
  sex_ratio_19 + Population_density_19 + m_age_2017 + offset(log(Pop_2019)),
  data = su, link = log)
car::vif(b1)
b2 <- step(b1, trace = 0)
summary(b2)

# residual diagnostics
plot(simulateResiduals(fittedModel = b2))
Results
Final negative binomial model retained age, education, hypertension, financial independence and population density (all p < 0.05 before spatial smoothing).


Spatial autocorrelation and clustering


Neighbours were defined as each municipality’s five nearest neighbours (symmetrised, row-standardised weights).



Global Moran’s I = 0.447, p = 0.001 (999 Monte Carlo permutations). Municipalities with high mortality tend to neighbour other high-mortality municipalities, and the same holds for low values.









85 of 250 municipalities have a local Moran p-value below 0.1 (65 below 0.05).


R code · the spatial analysis
# boundaries (the sp/rgdal workflow used originally; sf::st_read() is the modern equivalent)
ROK <- rgdal::readOGR("final_korea_202005(20201114).shp", encoding = "utf-8")
ROK.sf <- st_as_sf(ROK)
ROK <- spTransform(ROK, "+init=epsg:4326")
ROK@data$SIG_CD <- as.factor(ROK@data$SIG_CD)
su$SIG_CD <- as.factor(su$SIG_CD)
ROK@data <- dplyr::left_join(ROK@data, su, by = "SIG_CD")

# spatial weights: 5 nearest neighbours, symmetrised, row-standardised
coord <- coordinates(ROK)
pp <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coord, k = 5), sym = TRUE)
wt <- nb2listw(pp, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# global Moran's I (999 Monte Carlo simulations)
moran.mc(ROK@data$Pneumonia19, listw = wt, nsim = 999, na.action = na.exclude)
moran.plot(ROK@data$Pneumonia19, listw = wt)

# local Moran's I and LISA clusters (significance threshold 0.1)
local1 <- localmoran(ROK@data$Pneumonia19, listw = nb2listw(pp, style = "W"))
quadrant <- vector("numeric", nrow(local1))
m.x <- ROK@data$Pneumonia19 - mean(ROK@data$Pneumonia19)
m.l <- local1[, 1] - mean(local1[, 1])
quadrant[m.x < 0 & m.l < 0] <- 1   # low-low
quadrant[m.x < 0 & m.l > 0] <- 2   # low-high
quadrant[m.x > 0 & m.l < 0] <- 3   # high-low
quadrant[m.x > 0 & m.l > 0] <- 4   # high-high
quadrant[local1[, 5] > 0.1] <- 0   # not significant
colors <- c("white", "blue", rgb(0, 0, 1, alpha = 0.4), rgb(1, 0, 0, alpha = 0.4), "red")
plot(ROK, border = "lightgray", col = colors[findInterval(quadrant, 0:4)])


Bayesian hierarchical spatial models


To account for residual spatial dependence, three negative binomial models were fitted with INLA: a non-spatial GLM, a Besag (ICAR) spatial model, and a BYM model combining spatially structured and unstructured random effects. The BYM model used penalised-complexity priors, P(σ > 0.5) = 0.01, and a contiguity-based neighbourhood. Predictors: financial independence, education below high school, hypertension, population density, mean age and sex ratio.



Model comparison (lower is better)

ModelDICWAIC


GLM (non-spatial)2488.52493.3


Besag ICAR2457.62473.1


BYM (PC priors)2227.62205.5




The BYM model is clearly preferred. It uses many effective parameters (about 198 by DIC), so the random effects absorb a lot of municipality-level variation. The unstructured-effect variance is 0.118 (95% CrI 0.092–0.163).



BYM model: fixed effects (per 1 SD of each predictor)

PredictorPosterior mean95% CrIRelative risk (95% CrI)


Financial independence−0.165−0.257, −0.0740.848 (0.774–0.928)


Education below high school0.050−0.054, 0.1551.052 (0.948–1.167)


Hypertension prevalence0.1090.028, 0.1901.115 (1.029–1.209)


Population density−0.212−0.297, −0.128n/a


Mean age0.4540.353, 0.555n/a


Sex ratio0.049−0.033, 0.131n/a




Shaded rows have credible intervals that exclude zero. Relative risks were computed for the three predictors of interest. The Besag model gives very similar values: financial independence 0.854 (0.779–0.936), hypertension 1.122 (1.035–1.217), education 1.061 (0.950–1.186).


Reading the results. Municipalities one standard deviation higher in financial independence have about 15% lower pneumonia mortality, and those one standard deviation higher in hypertension prevalence have about 12% higher mortality, after accounting for age structure, density and spatial dependence. Education below high school points in the risky direction but its interval includes 1.


Model validation








R code · the INLA models
# contiguity graph for INLA
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
ROK_nb <- poly2nb(ROK.sf)
nb2INLA("ROK.graph", ROK_nb)
ROK.adj <- paste(getwd(), "/ROK.graph", sep = "")
ROK@data$idarea <- 1:nrow(ROK@data)

# penalised-complexity prior: P(sigma > 0.5) = 0.01 for both BYM components
hyperbym <- list(prec.unstruct = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.5, 0.01)),
                 prec.spatial  = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.5, 0.01)))

covs <- "Fin_ind_2019 + Per_below_highsch_2019 + Percent_hypertension_2019 +
         Population_density_19 + m_age_2017 + sex_ratio_19 + offset(log(Pop_2019))"
f0 <- as.formula(paste("Pneumonia_deaths ~", covs))                                  # GLM
f  <- as.formula(paste("Pneumonia_deaths ~", covs,
  "+ f(idarea, model = 'besag', graph = ROK.adj, scale.model = TRUE)"))              # Besag ICAR
f1 <- as.formula(paste("Pneumonia_deaths ~", covs,
  "+ f(idarea, model = 'bym', graph = ROK.adj, scale.model = TRUE, hyper = hyperbym)")) # BYM

# NOTE: as run originally. The covariates were already standardised (see above), so as.integer()
# truncates them toward zero. This may not be intended.
cov_names <- c("sex_ratio_19","m_age_2017","Highrisk_drk_2019","smk_cur_p_2019","Passive_smk_househ_2019",
  "Passive_smk_workpl_2019","Reg_exercise_2019","Per_below_highsch_2019","Fin_ind_2019","Perc_Single_2019",
  "doc_per1000_17","Percent_hypertension_2019","Percent_diabetes_2019","Obesity_prev_2019",
  "Unmet_medical_facilities_2019","PM10_2019","Pneumonia19","Pneumonia_deaths",
  "Population_density_19","Old_age_popn")
ROK@data <- ROK@data %>% mutate_at(cov_names, as.integer)

ctl <- list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
r0 <- inla(f0, data = ROK@data, family = "nbinomial", control.compute = ctl, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
r  <- inla(f,  data = ROK@data, family = "nbinomial", control.compute = ctl, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
r1 <- inla(f1, data = ROK@data, family = "nbinomial", control.compute = ctl, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

data.frame(dic = c(r0$dic$dic, r$dic$dic, r1$dic$dic),
           waic = c(r0$waic$waic, r$waic$waic, r1$waic$waic),
           row.names = c("GLM", "Besag ICAR", "BYM"))

# relative risks (per 1 SD): posterior of exp(beta)
rr <- function(m, v) inla.qmarginal(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
        inla.tmarginal(exp, m$marginals.fixed[[v]]))
rr(r1, "Fin_ind_2019"); rr(r1, "Percent_hypertension_2019"); rr(r1, "Per_below_highsch_2019")
Results
BYM model (best fit, DIC 2228)
  • Financial independence → RR 0.85 (protective)
  • Hypertension prevalence → RR 1.12 (risk)
  • Older mean age associated with higher mortality
  • Lower population density associated with higher mortality


Spatio-temporal extension, 2015–2019


The same municipalities were followed over five years (250 × 5 = 1,250 observations). The model adds a common linear time trend and municipality-specific slopes to the BYM spatial effect.










Spatio-temporal BYM model: fixed effects (raw, unstandardised units)

TermPosterior mean95% CrIRelative risk (95% CrI)


Year (linear trend)0.1280.119, 0.1371.137 (1.126–1.147) per year


Financial independence−0.010−0.014, −0.0050.991 (0.986–0.995) per 1 point


Hypertension prevalence0.016−0.006, 0.0381.016 (0.994–1.038) per 1 point


Education below high school−0.001−0.022, 0.0200.999 (0.978–1.020) per 1 point


Mean age0.0850.064, 0.1061.089 per year of age




Year and age rate ratios were calculated as exp() of the printed coefficients (and interval limits). Population density and sex ratio are not shown (effects near zero on this scale).


Expected deaths increased steadily over the period (about 14% per year), and financial independence stays protective. Hypertension, which was clearly associated in the 2019 cross-section, has an interval that includes 1 here.



R code · the spatio-temporal model
dat <- read.csv("ST_pnu.csv")          # long format: 250 municipalities x 2015-2019
# `map` = boundary file joined to the wide-format data (see the Rmd)
nb <- poly2nb(map); nb2INLA("map.adj", nb); g <- inla.read.graph("map.adj")
dat$idarea  <- as.numeric(as.factor(dat$SIG_CD))
dat$idarea1 <- dat$idarea
dat$idtime  <- 1 + dat$Year - min(dat$Year)

formula <- Pneumonia ~ Fin_ind_2019 + Per_below_highsch_2019 + Percent_hypertension_2019 +
  Population_density_19 + m_age_2017 + sex_ratio_19 + offset(log(Pop_2019)) +
  f(idarea, model = "bym", graph = g) +       # spatial effect
  f(idarea1, idtime, model = "iid") + idtime  # area-specific slopes + common linear trend

res <- inla(formula, family = "nbinomial", data = dat, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
summary(res)
Results
2015–2019 trend
  • Expected deaths rose ~14% per year (RR 1.14)
  • Financial independence remained protective
  • Mean age remained a risk factor


Conclusion
Clustering
  • Pneumonia mortality is positively spatially autocorrelated (Moran’s I 0.447, p = 0.001). High-high clusters are in the north-east and central regions; 85 of 250 municipalities had local p below 0.1.
2019 models
  • In the final negative binomial model, higher mortality went with older mean age (RR 1.33), lower education (1.12) and hypertension (1.07), and lower mortality with higher financial independence (0.92) and population density (0.84).
  • The BYM model fitted best (DIC 2227.6, against 2457.6 for Besag and 2488.5 for the non-spatial model). In it, financial independence was protective (RR 0.848, 0.774–0.928) and hypertension was a risk factor (1.115, 1.029–1.209). Mean age was higher and population density lower in high-mortality areas, both with intervals excluding zero.
  • Education below high school (1.052) and sex ratio were not significant after spatial smoothing.
2015–2019 trend
  • Expected deaths rose about 14% per year (RR 1.137, 1.126–1.147).
  • Financial independence stayed protective (0.991 per point) and mean age remained a risk factor (1.089 per year). Hypertension (1.016) and education (0.999) were not significant in this model.
